The response part is what makes EDR different: from the console an analyst can isolate the host from the network while keeping the management channel open, kill a process, quarantine a file, pull a file for analysis, or run a remote shell. Isolation in seconds is what stops ransomware spreading from one branch PC to the file server.

Extended detection and response (XDR). XDR takes the EDR model and widens the sensors: endpoint plus email gateway, identity provider, cloud workloads, firewall and network. The point is correlation. A single alert of a suspicious login from a new country is low priority; the same login followed by a mailbox forwarding rule being created and a large download from SharePoint is a clear account compromise. XDR stitches these into one incident with a timeline. It differs from a SIEM in that it is typically a single vendor's integrated platform with built-in detections and response actions, whereas a SIEM ingests any log source and needs rules to be written.

Network access control (NAC). NAC decides whether a device may join the network at all. Using IEEE 802.1X, the switch port or wireless access point stays closed until the device authenticates through a RADIUS server, usually with a certificate or domain credentials. NAC can also perform a posture check: is the EDR agent running, is the disk encrypted, are patches current? A device that fails goes to a quarantine VLAN with access only to remediation servers. Agentless NAC uses profiling to identify devices such as printers or IP phones and assigns them to the right VLAN. NAC is the control that stops a visitor's infected laptop or a rogue device plugged into a branch wall port from touching the core network.

User behaviour analytics (UBA or UEBA). Rather than looking for known bad, UBA builds a baseline of what is normal for each user and entity: which systems they touch, at what hours, from where, and how much data they move. It then scores deviations. A teller who normally views 40 accounts a day suddenly querying 4,000, or a service account logging in interactively at 03:00 from a workstation for the first time, raises a risk score even though no single event broke a rule. UBA is especially good at insider threat and at compromised credentials, where the attacker's actions are technically authorised. It is typically a module within a SIEM or XDR platform.

On the job. Bank SOC analysts spend much of the day in the EDR console: triaging detections, checking process trees, isolating hosts and hunting across the estate for indicators. NAC posture failures are a routine helpdesk queue. GRC teams cite EDR coverage percentages and NAC enforcement as key controls in CBN cybersecurity framework self-assessments.

keyTerms.def: An endpoint agent and console that continuously records device activity, detects malicious behaviour and lets analysts respond remotely, including isolating the host.
A platform that correlates telemetry from endpoints, email, identity, cloud and network into unified incidents with coordinated response.
An EDR action that cuts a device's network access except to the management console, stopping lateral movement.
A system that authenticates devices and checks their security posture before granting network access, often using 802.1X.
The port-based network access control standard in which a supplicant authenticates through an authenticator to a RADIUS server.
A NAC check of a device's security state, such as patch level and running antivirus, before allowing full access.
Analytics that baseline normal activity for users and entities and flag anomalies that may indicate insider threat or compromised accounts.
A restricted network segment to which non-compliant devices are placed until they are remediated.

examTips: EDR is the answer when the scenario asks to detect fileless or unknown malware by behaviour, or to isolate a host remotely.
XDR is the answer when the scenario needs correlation across endpoint, email and identity in one platform.
NAC and 802.1X are the answer when the problem is unauthorised or non-compliant devices connecting to the network.
UBA is the answer when a legitimate user's account is behaving abnormally and no signature or rule would catch it.
videos.realWorld: A common Nigerian bank incident: a branch user opens a macro-enabled invoice, and EDR flags Excel spawning PowerShell with an encoded command. The analyst isolates the machine from the console, reviews the process tree, extracts the downloaded payload hash, and searches the whole estate for it. NAC logs confirm no other device on that VLAN was non-compliant. Weeks later, UBA flags the same user's account accessing customer records at unusual volumes from a different branch, which turns out to be credentials stolen during the original incident and not rotated.

quiz.q: A SOC analyst sees an alert that a workstation is encrypting files rapidly and attempting SMB connections to the file server. Which action, available through the endpoint security platform, most quickly limits the spread?
options: Run a vulnerability scan against the host
Isolate the host from the network using EDR
Move the host to a quarantine VLAN using NAC posture policy
quiz.explain: EDR host isolation immediately blocks all network traffic except the management channel, stopping lateral movement in seconds. Signature updates are too slow, NAC quarantine typically triggers only at connection time, and scanning does not stop an active attack.

quiz.q: A bank wants to prevent employees and visitors from plugging personal laptops into wall ports in branch offices and reaching the internal network. Which technology best meets this requirement?
quiz.explain: NAC with 802.1X keeps the switch port closed until the device authenticates, and can enforce posture checks. UBA and XDR detect and respond after access is gained, and FIM watches file changes.

quiz.q: A customer service agent's credentials are valid and no malware is present, yet the account begins accessing ten times its usual number of customer records outside normal working hours. Which capability is designed to detect this type of activity?
quiz.explain: UBA baselines normal behaviour per user and flags statistical deviations even when every action is technically authorised. Antivirus needs a malicious file, NAC controls device admission, and DNS filtering controls name resolution.

objectives.title: Given a scenario, implement and maintain identity and access management

videos.title: Identity and Access Management
videos.summary: Messer covers the identity lifecycle from provisioning to deprovisioning, permission assignment, identity proofing, federation and single sign-on with LDAP, OAuth and SAML, plus interoperability and attestation.
videos.deepDive:
Identity and access management (IAM) is the set of processes and systems that answer two questions for every request: who are you, and what are you allowed to do? Most breaches in financial services trace back to an identity problem: an orphaned account, an over-privileged user, or a stolen credential. The exam tests the lifecycle and the protocols that make identity portable.

Provisioning and deprovisioning. Provisioning creates the account and grants its initial access when someone joins; deprovisioning disables and eventually deletes it when they leave or change roles. The best practice is to drive both from the HR system of record. When HR marks a new teller as hired, an identity governance tool automatically creates the Active Directory account, adds it to the teller role group, and provisions the core banking profile. When HR records a termination, the same workflow disables everything within minutes. Manual deprovisioning is where banks fail audits: a contractor's VPN account still active a year after the contract ended is a classic finding. Role changes need attention too, because access tends to accumulate as people move departments, which is called privilege creep.

Permission assignments. Assign permissions to roles or groups, never directly to individuals, and follow least privilege: the minimum access needed to do the job. Group-based assignment makes provisioning repeatable and makes reviews possible, because you review a role's permissions once rather than a thousand users' individual entitlements.

Identity proofing. Before an account is issued, the organisation must confirm the person is who they claim. For staff this means HR verification of identity documents; for customers it is KYC: government ID, BVN and NIN checks in Nigeria, liveness-checked selfies, and address verification. Proofing also covers the password-reset path, since an attacker who can convince the helpdesk they are the CFO gets everything. Strong proofing at reset time is as important as at enrolment.

Federation and single sign-on. Federation lets one organisation trust identities issued by another, so a user authenticates once at their home identity provider (IdP) and is accepted by multiple service providers (SPs). Single sign-on (SSO) is the user-facing result: log in once, reach many applications. Three protocols appear on the exam. LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) is how applications query a directory such as Active Directory for users, groups and attributes; it is the backbone of internal authentication but is not itself a web SSO protocol. SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) is XML-based web SSO: the SP redirects the browser to the IdP, the IdP authenticates the user and returns a signed assertion listing who they are and their attributes, and the SP trusts it. SAML is the standard for enterprise SaaS. OAuth 2.0 is an authorisation framework: it issues access tokens that let one application act on a user's behalf with another, such as a budgeting app reading your bank transactions through Open Banking without holding your bank password. OpenID Connect adds an identity layer on top of OAuth so it can be used for login, and it is what powers sign in with Google.

Interoperability and attestation. Interoperability means choosing standards so that the IdP, the HR system, the cloud apps and the on-premises directory all work together, usually via SAML, OIDC and SCIM for automated provisioning. Attestation is the periodic review in which managers certify that each person's access is still appropriate; access that nobody attests to is removed. Quarterly attestation of privileged and financial system access is expected by CBN and by ISO 27001 auditors.

On the job. GRC analysts run the attestation campaigns and track orphaned accounts as findings. SOC analysts watch for logins to disabled accounts, SAML assertions from unexpected IdPs, and OAuth consent grants to unknown third-party apps, which is a modern phishing technique.

keyTerms.def: Creating an identity and granting its initial access, ideally triggered automatically from the HR system.
Disabling and removing an identity's access promptly when the person leaves or no longer needs it.
Verifying that a person is who they claim to be before issuing or resetting credentials.
A trust arrangement in which one organisation accepts identities authenticated by another organisation's identity provider.
An XML-based standard in which an identity provider sends a signed assertion about a user to a service provider for web single sign-on.
An authorisation framework that issues tokens allowing one application limited access to a user's resources on another without sharing the password.
A protocol for querying and modifying directory services such as Active Directory, used by applications to look up users and groups.
A periodic review in which owners or managers confirm that each user's access remains appropriate.
The gradual accumulation of access rights as a user changes roles without old permissions being removed.

examTips: SAML is for web SSO with an identity provider issuing assertions; OAuth is for delegated authorisation with tokens; LDAP is for directory queries. Match the protocol to the verb in the question.
If a former employee's account is still active, the failure is deprovisioning; if a current employee has access from an old role, it is missing attestation or privilege creep.
Identity proofing happens before credentials are issued and again at password reset; it is not the same as authentication.
Federation lets users authenticate at their home organisation and access a partner's resources without a separate account.
videos.realWorld: A GRC analyst at a Lagos fintech runs a quarterly access review: the tool pulls every account in Active Directory, the core banking system and AWS, matches them to HR records, and flags twelve accounts belonging to people no longer employed and thirty users whose entitlements exceed their role. Managers attest or revoke through the portal, the analyst tracks completion, and the evidence pack goes to internal audit and, when asked, to CBN examiners. The SOC separately alerts on any login attempt against one of the disabled accounts.

quiz.q: An audit discovers that a contractor who left a bank eight months ago still has an active VPN account and access to the ticketing system. Which IAM process failed?
quiz.explain: Deprovisioning is the timely removal of access when a person leaves. Proofing concerns verifying identity at enrolment, federation concerns cross-organisation trust, and permission assignment concerns what access is granted while the account is legitimate.

quiz.q: A company wants its employees to log in once with their corporate credentials and then access several cloud SaaS applications without separate passwords. The SaaS vendors must accept signed identity assertions from the corporate identity provider. Which protocol is most appropriate?
quiz.explain: SAML is the standard for web single sign-on where an identity provider issues signed assertions to service providers. LDAP queries directories, RADIUS authenticates network access, and SNMPv3 is for device management.

quiz.q: A third-party budgeting app asks a customer to grant it permission to read their transaction history from the bank's API without ever receiving the customer's online banking password. Which framework enables this?
quiz.explain: OAuth 2.0 issues scoped access tokens that let a third-party application act on a user's behalf without sharing credentials. Kerberos and TACACS+ are authentication protocols for internal networks and devices, and LDAPS is encrypted directory access.

videos.title: Access Controls
videos.summary: Messer compares the access control models: mandatory, discretionary, role-based, rule-based, attribute-based and time-of-day restrictions, all built on least privilege.
videos.deepDive:
Once a system knows who you are, an access control model decides what you can touch. The exam gives you a scenario and asks which model is in play or which one to choose. The trick is to notice who makes the decision and what the decision is based on.

Least privilege is the principle underneath all of them: give each user, process or service only the rights required for its task, for only as long as needed. A backup service account needs read access to data and write access to the backup target, not domain admin. The models below are different ways of implementing that principle.

Discretionary access control (DAC). The owner of a resource decides who can access it. Windows NTFS permissions and Linux file modes are DAC: if you create a file, you can share it with anyone. It is flexible and easy, which is also the problem, because users share too widely and there is no central guarantee of policy. A spreadsheet of customer data that its owner sets to Everyone: Read is a DAC failure.

Mandatory access control (MAC). A central authority sets policy and users cannot override it. Every object carries a classification label (such as Top Secret, Secret, Confidential) and every subject carries a clearance; the system permits access only when clearance dominates classification, and even the owner cannot grant access to someone with insufficient clearance. It is used in military systems and in SELinux. Exam signal: the words label, clearance or classification mean MAC.

Role-based access control (RBAC). Permissions attach to roles, and users are assigned roles. A bank defines roles such as Teller, Branch Manager, Loan Officer and Auditor; the Teller role can post deposits up to a limit, the Branch Manager role can approve reversals, the Auditor role can read everything and change nothing. Onboarding a new teller is simply assigning the Teller role. RBAC is the dominant enterprise model because it scales and maps directly to job functions and to attestation reviews. It also enables separation of duties: the person who creates a payment cannot be in the role that approves it.

Rule-based access control. Access is granted or denied according to system-wide rules, regardless of who the user is. A firewall ACL is rule-based. So is a policy that says no file downloads over 100 MB, or that all access from outside Nigeria is denied. The distinguishing feature is that the rule applies uniformly and is evaluated on each access.

Attribute-based access control (ABAC). Decisions combine multiple attributes of the subject, the object, the action and the environment: department equals treasury AND device is managed AND location is a branch AND time is within working hours AND data classification is internal. ABAC is the most granular and is how modern cloud policies (AWS IAM condition keys, Azure conditional access) work. It is powerful but harder to audit than RBAC because the effective permissions depend on context.

Time-of-day restrictions. A simple but effective rule: teller accounts can only log in between 07:00 and 19:00 on business days; a logon at 02:00 is denied and alerted. Attackers work when staff are asleep, so this control removes a large window. It can be a standalone setting in Active Directory or an attribute inside an ABAC policy.

Putting it together. Real systems mix models. A bank's core application uses RBAC for job functions, time-of-day limits for branch staff, rule-based network controls at the firewall, and conditional (attribute-based) policies in the cloud identity platform, with DAC still governing personal files on shares. A SOC analyst needs to know which layer denied a request when investigating; a GRC analyst needs to show that the role definitions enforce separation of duties and least privilege, which CBN and PCI DSS both require.

keyTerms.def: Granting a subject only the access strictly needed to perform its function and nothing more.
A model in which the resource owner decides who may access it, as with NTFS and Unix file permissions.
A model in which a central policy using classification labels and clearances controls access and owners cannot override it.
A model in which permissions are assigned to job roles and users receive access by being assigned roles.
A model in which system-wide rules, such as firewall ACLs, determine access regardless of the identity of the user.
A model that evaluates attributes of the user, resource, action and environment together to make each access decision.
A control that permits logon or access only during defined hours or days.
Splitting a sensitive task across roles so that no single person can complete it alone.

examTips: Owner decides means DAC; labels and clearances mean MAC; job function means RBAC; firewall-style conditions mean rule-based; multiple contextual factors mean ABAC.
RBAC is the usual answer for enterprise scalability and for enforcing separation of duties.
ABAC is the answer when the scenario mentions device state, location, time and department all at once.
Least privilege is a principle, not a model; a question may ask for the principle a control implements.
videos.realWorld: When a bank builds its role catalogue for a new core banking platform, GRC and business owners sit together to define what a Teller, Supervisor and Auditor may do and to document which combinations are toxic, such as create and approve payments. The SOC then writes detections on the identity platform: logins outside permitted hours, a user holding two conflicting roles, or a conditional access policy being bypassed from an unmanaged device. Both teams use these definitions during quarterly attestation and in responses to CBN examination questions on access governance.

quiz.q: A bank assigns permissions to job functions such as Teller, Supervisor and Auditor, and grants access to employees by placing them in the appropriate function. Which access control model is being used?
quiz.explain: Permissions tied to job functions and assigned to users through those functions is role-based access control. DAC lets owners decide, MAC uses classification labels, and ABAC evaluates many contextual attributes.

quiz.q: A government system labels every document as Confidential, Secret or Top Secret, and users can only open documents at or below their clearance level. Document owners cannot grant exceptions. Which model does this describe?
quiz.explain: Classification labels, clearances and the inability of owners to override the policy are the defining features of mandatory access control.

quiz.q: A fintech requires that treasury staff can access the payments portal only from company-managed devices, only from within Nigeria, and only during business hours, with all three conditions evaluated on every request. Which access control model best describes this policy?
quiz.explain: Combining device state, location and time attributes into one dynamic decision is attribute-based access control. RBAC alone considers only the role, MAC uses labels, and DAC leaves the decision to owners.

videos.title: Multifactor Authentication
videos.summary: Messer explains the authentication factors of something you know, have and are, plus somewhere you are, and the technologies behind them: biometrics, hard and soft tokens, and security keys.
videos.deepDive:
A password alone proves only that someone knows a secret, and secrets leak through phishing, reuse and database breaches. Multifactor authentication (MFA) requires evidence from two or more independent categories, so that stealing one does not grant access. The exam tests the categories, the technologies, and their weaknesses.

The factors. Something you know: a password, PIN or security question answer. Something you have: a physical or logical object such as a smart card, hardware token, phone running an authenticator app, or a FIDO2 security key. Something you are: a biometric, meaning fingerprint, face, iris, voice or vein pattern. The objectives also list somewhere you are: location derived from IP geolocation, GPS or the cell network, used mostly as a risk signal or to deny impossible travel. Two passwords are not MFA because both are the same factor; a password plus a code from an authenticator app is MFA because knowledge and possession are independent.

Biometrics. A biometric system enrols a template, then compares a live sample against it. Two error rates matter: the false rejection rate (FRR), when a legitimate user is denied, and the false acceptance rate (FAR), when an impostor is accepted. Tightening the threshold lowers FAR but raises FRR; the crossover error rate (CER) is where they are equal and is used to compare systems. Biometrics cannot be changed if compromised, so the template must be protected, and liveness detection is needed against photos and masks. Fingerprint and face are convenient and now standard on phones, which is why Nigerian banks use them for app login combined with device binding.

Hard and soft tokens. A hard token is a dedicated device: a key fob showing a six-digit code that changes every 30 seconds (time-based one-time password, TOTP) or on each press (HMAC-based, HOTP), or a smart card holding a certificate. A soft token is the same one-time-password algorithm implemented in an app such as Microsoft Authenticator or Google Authenticator on the user's phone, seeded with a secret at enrolment. Push notifications are a soft-token variant where the app asks approve or deny. Push is vulnerable to MFA fatigue attacks, where the attacker spams prompts until the user taps approve; number matching, where the user must type a code shown on the login screen, mitigates this. SMS codes count as possession but are the weakest option because of SIM swapping, a live problem in Nigeria where fraudsters obtain replacement SIMs to intercept bank OTPs.

Security keys. A FIDO2 or WebAuthn security key such as a YubiKey stores a private key and signs a challenge that includes the website's origin. Because the signature is bound to the real domain, a phishing site cannot replay it, which makes security keys the only common MFA method that is genuinely phishing-resistant. They are the right answer when a question emphasises resistance to phishing or credential replay. Passkeys bring the same protocol to phones and laptops using the device's own secure hardware.

Choosing. Rank by strength: security key or passkey, then authenticator app with number matching, then TOTP, then push without matching, then SMS or email. For high-value actions such as bulk payments, step-up authentication asks for a stronger factor at the moment of the transaction, not just at login.

On the job. SOC analysts investigate MFA push floods, SIM-swap fraud patterns and logins that succeeded from a new device without MFA, which usually means a legacy protocol bypass. GRC verifies MFA coverage for all remote access and privileged accounts, which CBN, PCI DSS 8.4 and cyber-insurance questionnaires all require.

keyTerms.def: Requiring evidence from two or more independent categories, such as knowledge and possession, to authenticate.
A possession factor such as a hardware token, smart card, authenticator app or security key.
An inherence factor based on a biometric characteristic such as a fingerprint or face.
A location factor derived from IP geolocation, GPS or network data, usually used as a risk signal.
Time-based one-time password, a code derived from a shared secret and the current time, changing every 30 seconds.
The proportion of impostor attempts a biometric system wrongly accepts.
The point where a biometric system's false acceptance and false rejection rates are equal, used to compare accuracy.
A hardware authenticator that signs an origin-bound challenge, making it resistant to phishing and replay.
An attack that floods a user with push approval requests hoping one is accepted by mistake.

examTips: Two items from the same category, such as a password and a PIN, are not multifactor.
Phishing-resistant MFA means FIDO2 security keys or passkeys; TOTP codes can be phished in real time.
SMS one-time codes are possession but the weakest form because of SIM swapping and interception.
For biometric questions, lowering FAR raises FRR; the CER compares systems.
videos.realWorld: A Nigerian fintech sees a spike in account takeovers where the attacker already has the customer's password and the SMS OTP is arriving on a SIM the fraudster obtained through a SIM swap at a telecom outlet. The SOC correlates the takeovers with recent SIM-change events from the telco feed and blocks transactions for 24 hours after any SIM change. On the corporate side, the same company moves administrators from push notifications to FIDO2 keys after an MFA fatigue attack nearly succeeded against a cloud engineer at 1 a.m.

quiz.q: Several employees have approved fraudulent MFA push notifications after being bombarded with dozens of prompts late at night. Which change most directly addresses this attack?
options: Add a second password to the login process
Require number matching or migrate to FIDO2 security keys
quiz.explain: Number matching forces the user to enter a code from the login screen, defeating blind approvals, and security keys remove the prompt entirely. SMS is weaker, password changes do not affect the MFA step, and two passwords are still a single factor.

quiz.q: A bank issues each administrator a hardware device that displays a new six-digit code every 30 seconds, used together with a password. Which combination of factors is this?
options: Something you know and something you have
Two instances of something you have
Something you know and something you are
Something you have and somewhere you are
quiz.explain: The password is knowledge and the TOTP hardware token is possession, giving two independent factors. No biometric or location element is involved.

quiz.q: A security team must choose an MFA method that cannot be defeated by a real-time phishing proxy that relays the user's credentials and one-time code to the legitimate site. Which option meets the requirement?
quiz.explain: A FIDO2 key signs a challenge that includes the genuine site's origin, so a proxy on a look-alike domain cannot obtain a valid signature. TOTP, SMS and simple push approvals can all be relayed by a phishing proxy.

videos.title: Password Security
videos.summary: Messer covers password best practices for length, complexity, reuse, expiration and age, and then password managers, passwordless authentication and privileged access management with just-in-time access, vaulting and ephemeral credentials.
videos.deepDive:
Passwords are still the most common credential, and most of them are weak, reused or already leaked. This video covers what good password policy looks like now (which is different from the advice of ten years ago), the tools that remove the burden from users, and how privileged accounts should be handled differently from everyone else.

Length, complexity and the modern view. Length beats complexity. An attacker with a stolen hash database tries billions of guesses per second, and each extra character multiplies the work more than swapping an o for a 0 does. NIST SP 800-63B now recommends a minimum of 8 characters (15 for single-factor), allowing up to at least 64, permitting spaces so users can choose passphrases, and not forcing composition rules like one uppercase, one symbol, because those push people toward predictable patterns such as Password1!. Instead, screen new passwords against lists of breached and common passwords and reject any that appear. The exam may still present complexity as a valid control, so recognise it, but know that length and breach-screening are the stronger answers.

Reuse, expiration and age. Reuse is the killer: credentials stolen from a shopping site are tried against the bank's webmail in credential-stuffing attacks. Password history settings (remember the last 24) prevent reuse within a system, and breach-list screening catches reuse across systems. Expiration used to be 90 days; NIST now says do not force periodic changes, because users respond with Lagos2024 becoming Lagos2025, and instead change passwords only when compromise is suspected. Minimum password age (for example one day) exists to stop users cycling through 24 quick changes to get back to their favourite. Account lockout after a number of failures limits online guessing; be careful, because lockout can be abused to lock out staff deliberately.

Password managers. A password manager generates a unique random password per site, stores them in a vault encrypted under one strong master password (plus MFA), and fills them in automatically. This removes reuse and weak choices at once, and the autofill only works on the genuine domain, which incidentally blocks phishing look-alikes. Enterprise password managers add sharing of team credentials with audit trails and revocation when someone leaves.

Passwordless. Passwordless authentication replaces the memorised secret with a possession or biometric factor: FIDO2 passkeys, Windows Hello for Business, smart cards, or a phone-based approval bound to the device. There is nothing to phish, reuse or leak from a database. It is the direction the industry is going and the answer when a question wants to eliminate password-based attacks entirely.

Privileged access management (PAM). Administrator, root, database and service accounts can do the most damage, so they get their own controls. Password vaulting stores privileged credentials in a PAM system; administrators check out a credential for a session, the session is recorded, and the vault rotates the password immediately afterwards so the human never keeps a working one. Just-in-time (JIT) access means privileges do not exist standing; an engineer requests elevation for a task, an approver or policy grants it for two hours, and it is removed automatically. Standing domain admin membership is the thing attackers most want to find, and JIT removes it. Ephemeral credentials are short-lived by design: a cloud role that issues a token valid for 15 minutes, an SSH certificate that expires at the end of the day. Even if captured, they are useless soon after.

On the job. SOC analysts hunt credential stuffing by watching for many failed logins across many accounts from few IPs, and they watch PAM session recordings during investigations. GRC teams write the password standard, evidence PAM coverage for privileged accounts, and answer CBN and PCI DSS 8.3 questions on password parameters.

keyTerms.def: The number of characters in a password, the single largest factor in resistance to offline cracking.
Composition rules requiring character classes such as upper case, numbers and symbols, now considered less effective than length.
Forcing a change after a set period, no longer recommended by NIST except when compromise is suspected.
The shortest time a password must be kept before it can be changed, preventing rapid cycling to bypass history rules.
Using username and password pairs leaked from one breach to log in to other services where users reused them.
Software that generates, stores and fills unique random passwords from an encrypted vault protected by a master credential.
Authenticating with possession or biometric factors such as passkeys, removing the memorised secret entirely.
Granting privileged rights only when requested for a task and automatically removing them afterwards.
Storing privileged credentials in a PAM system that checks them out for sessions and rotates them afterwards.
A credential that is valid only for a short time or a single session so that its theft has little value.

examTips: Length is more important than complexity; passphrases and breached-password screening are the modern answer.
If the scenario is many failed logins across many accounts from one source, that is credential stuffing or password spraying; the answers involve MFA, lockout and breach screening.
Standing administrator rights should be replaced with just-in-time elevation; that phrase is the answer for reducing privileged exposure.
Password vaulting with automatic rotation is the PAM control for shared or service account credentials.
videos.realWorld: After a leak of a Nigerian e-commerce site's user database, a bank's SOC sees thousands of login attempts against its customer portal using the leaked email addresses, with a small percentage succeeding because customers reused passwords. The team forces resets for matched accounts, tightens rate limiting and pushes app-based passkeys. Internally, the same bank moves all domain and database administrator credentials into a PAM vault, records every privileged session, and replaces standing domain admin rights with just-in-time elevation approved through the ticketing system.

quiz.q: A security team is updating the password standard. Which change most improves resistance to offline cracking of stolen password hashes while aligning with current NIST guidance?
options: Limit passwords to a maximum of 12 characters
Require a minimum length of 15 characters and screen against breached-password lists
Require at least one symbol and one number
quiz.explain: Length is the dominant factor in cracking resistance and breach-list screening prevents known-weak choices. Frequent expiration produces predictable variations, composition rules add little, and a low maximum length actively weakens security.

quiz.q: An organisation's database administrators hold permanent full privileges on production servers. A recent incident showed an attacker used a stolen DBA credential for weeks. Which control most directly reduces this risk?
options: Move the DBAs to a password manager
Implement just-in-time privileged access with automatic expiry
quiz.explain: Just-in-time access removes standing privileges so a stolen credential carries no rights outside an approved window. Complexity and history do not limit the duration of privilege, and a password manager addresses storage rather than standing access.

quiz.q: A company wants to eliminate phishing of employee passwords entirely rather than merely making passwords stronger. Which approach best meets this goal?
options: Deploy passwordless authentication with FIDO2 passkeys
quiz.explain: Passwordless authentication removes the memorised secret, so there is nothing for a phishing page to capture, and FIDO2 is origin-bound. Expiration, security questions and lockout thresholds all still depend on a phishable secret.

objectives.title: Explain the importance of automation and orchestration related to secure operations

videos.title: Scripting and Automation
videos.summary: Messer explains why security teams automate repetitive work, the common use cases from user provisioning to ticket creation and API integrations, the benefits, and the costs and risks such as complexity, single points of failure and technical debt.
videos.deepDive:
Security operations generate far more work than a team can do by hand: hundreds of alerts a day, dozens of joiners and leavers a week, thousands of cloud resources that must be configured identically. Scripting and orchestration turn documented procedures into code so that they run the same way every time, in seconds, without a person having to remember each step. The exam wants you to know the use cases, the benefits, and the honest downsides.

Use cases. User provisioning: when HR marks a hire, a script creates the directory account, assigns role groups, enrols MFA and sends onboarding instructions; on termination it disables everything within minutes, which is exactly the deprovisioning gap auditors keep finding. Resource provisioning: infrastructure as code (Terraform, CloudFormation, Ansible) builds servers, networks and cloud accounts from templates, so every environment carries the same hardening. Guard rails: automated policies that prevent or undo unsafe changes, such as a cloud rule that immediately blocks an S3 bucket set to public or refuses a security group open to 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22. Security groups: scripts manage firewall and cloud security group membership so that access is granted and revoked by policy rather than by manual edits. Ticket creation: a SIEM detection automatically opens a ticket with the relevant logs attached, assigned to the right queue. Escalation: if a critical ticket is untouched for 15 minutes, the workflow pages the on-call lead. Enabling and disabling services and access: automatically disable an account after a confirmed phishing click, or turn off a vulnerable service across a fleet. Continuous integration and continuous testing: every code commit triggers static analysis, dependency scanning and unit tests before it can be merged, so security checks run on every change and not just at annual review. Integrations and APIs: the glue for all of the above. A SOAR (security orchestration, automation and response) platform calls the EDR API to isolate a host, the identity provider API to reset a session, the threat intelligence API to enrich an indicator, and the ticketing API to record it all.

A worked playbook. A phishing report arrives in the SOC mailbox. The SOAR playbook parses the email, extracts URLs and attachment hashes, queries VirusTotal and the sandbox, checks the proxy logs for anyone who clicked, and if the verdict is malicious it deletes the message from every mailbox, blocks the domain on the web filter and DNS filter, forces a password reset and session revocation for users who clicked, opens a ticket with all the evidence, and notifies the analyst. What took an analyst 45 minutes now takes 90 seconds, and the analyst reviews and approves the high-impact steps instead of doing the clerical ones.

Benefits. Efficiency and time saved; enforcement of baselines because every build is identical; secure scaling, since one script handles one server or a thousand; employee retention, because analysts do not burn out on repetitive triage; reaction time measured in seconds rather than hours, which directly reduces the blast radius of ransomware; and a workforce multiplier for small teams, which describes most Nigerian bank SOCs.

Other considerations. Complexity: an orchestration of ten integrated tools is hard to understand and debug, and a wrong condition can disable a thousand accounts. Cost: platforms, licences and the engineers who build and maintain playbooks. Single point of failure: if the automation server or its API token fails, every dependent process stops, so it needs high availability and monitoring. Technical debt: quick scripts written during an incident, never documented, still running years later with hard-coded credentials. Ongoing supportability: APIs change, vendors are replaced, the person who wrote the script leaves; playbooks need owners, version control, testing and documentation like any production software. The exam answer to most automation risk questions is a combination of change management, testing in a non-production environment, human approval for destructive steps, and treating scripts as code with version control.

keyTerms.def: Coordinating multiple tools and steps into a single automated workflow, often through a SOAR platform.
Security orchestration, automation and response, a platform that runs playbooks integrating security tools through APIs.
A defined, often automated sequence of actions for handling a specific type of event, such as a phishing report.
Automated policies that prevent or automatically reverse unsafe configuration changes.
Defining servers, networks and cloud resources in versioned templates so they are provisioned consistently and automatically.
Automatically building and testing code on every commit so that security checks run continuously rather than periodically.
Application programming interface, the programmatic entry point that lets scripts and platforms control a tool.
The accumulated maintenance burden of quick or undocumented automation that becomes harder and riskier to change over time.
A component, such as an automation server, whose failure halts every process that depends on it.

examTips: Automation questions usually ask for the benefit: consistency, speed, scaling, reduced human error, or freeing analysts for higher-value work.
When the scenario describes a script that no one understands and everyone is afraid to touch, the term is technical debt.
Guard rails prevent misconfiguration automatically; they are the answer for stopping public cloud storage or open security groups.
For risk of automation going wrong, answers include testing, change control, version control and human approval for destructive actions.
videos.realWorld: A five-person SOC at a Lagos fintech was drowning in phishing reports until it built a SOAR playbook that enriches, scores and quarantines automatically, leaving analysts to approve only account resets. The same team learned the downside when a guard-rail script with an overly broad filter disabled the CFO's account during month-end close; the fix was a staging tenant for testing playbooks, code review for every change, and an approval step for any action touching more than five accounts. GRC now lists the automation platform as a critical system with its own backup and access review.

quiz.q: A SOC receives roughly 200 phishing reports per week, and each takes an analyst 40 minutes to enrich, scope and remediate. Which approach best addresses this workload while maintaining consistent handling?
options: Implement a SOAR playbook that automates enrichment, scoping and quarantine via tool APIs
Ask users to stop reporting suspicious emails
Extend the SLA for phishing tickets to five days
quiz.explain: Orchestration through APIs performs the repetitive steps in seconds and identically every time, scaling far better than adding headcount. Discouraging reports and extending SLAs increase risk.

quiz.q: An organisation relies on dozens of scripts written years ago by an engineer who has since left. The scripts are undocumented, contain embedded credentials, and no one is willing to modify them. Which term best describes this situation?
quiz.explain: Undocumented, unmaintained automation that has become risky and expensive to change is technical debt. A single point of failure is about availability, guard rails are preventive policies, and CI is a development practice.

quiz.q: A cloud engineer accidentally sets a storage bucket containing customer documents to public access. Which automation capability would have prevented or immediately reversed this?
quiz.explain: Guard rails are automated policies that block or revert unsafe configurations such as public storage. Ticketing and escalation only notify people, and user provisioning manages accounts.

videos.title: Incident Response
videos.summary: Messer walks through the incident response process: preparation, detection, analysis, containment, eradication, recovery and lessons learned.
videos.deepDive:
An incident is an event that actually harms or threatens confidentiality, integrity or availability: ransomware, a compromised account, a data leak. The incident response (IR) process, drawn from NIST SP 800-61, gives the team a repeatable path from first alert to closure. The exam tests the order of the phases and which activity belongs to which phase. Below the phases are applied to a ransomware case at a bank so each one is concrete.

1. Preparation. Everything you do before anything happens: an IR policy and plan, a named team with contact details and deputies, a communications plan including out-of-band channels (an attacker inside email can read your response emails), tooling such as EDR, SIEM, forensic workstations and clean media, tested backups, playbooks for common incidents, relationships with law enforcement, regulators and a retained forensic firm, and staff training. For a bank this also means knowing the CBN and NDPC reporting timelines in advance.

2. Detection. Something raises the flag: EDR alerts on mass file encryption at 02:10 on a Saturday, a branch calls to say every PC shows a ransom note, or a monitoring tool sees backups failing. Detection sources include the SIEM, EDR, user reports, third-party notifications and threat intelligence. Speed here depends on the monitoring built during preparation.

3. Analysis. Confirm it is real, then scope and prioritise. Which hosts are encrypted? Which account did the process run under? When did the first malicious logon happen? What is the entry point: a phishing email, an exposed RDP server, a vendor VPN? The team assigns severity based on impact (core banking down, customer data at risk) and decides who must be notified. Analysis and containment often run in parallel: you do not wait for full understanding before pulling the plug on the file server.

4. Containment. Stop the bleeding without destroying evidence. Short-term containment for ransomware: isolate affected hosts with EDR, disable the compromised accounts, block the attacker's command-and-control addresses at the firewall and DNS filter, and segment the branch network from the data centre. Long-term containment might mean rebuilding critical servers on a clean network segment while the investigation continues. Take forensic images and memory captures before wiping anything, because eradication destroys evidence.

5. Eradication. Remove the cause. Delete the malware and its persistence (scheduled tasks, services, registry run keys, rogue accounts), patch the exploited vulnerability, reset every credential the attacker could have seen including service accounts and Kerberos keys, and check for backdoors the attacker left. If you eradicate only the ransomware binary and not the initial access broker's web shell, the attacker returns.

6. Recovery. Restore operations safely: rebuild from known-good images, restore data from backups after verifying they are clean and predate the intrusion, bring systems back in priority order (payment switch before HR portal), and monitor closely for reinfection. Recovery includes confirming with the business that transactions reconcile.

7. Lessons learned. Within a week or two, hold a blameless review: what happened, what worked, what failed, what will change. Outputs are concrete actions with owners: enforce MFA on the vendor VPN, shorten backup verification cycles, add a detection for the persistence technique used. This feeds back into preparation, which is why the process is drawn as a cycle.

On the job. SOC analysts own detection and analysis and execute containment steps; incident managers coordinate; GRC handles regulatory notification (CBN, NDPC within 72 hours for personal data breaches), evidence retention and the lessons-learned report that goes to the board and to auditors.

keyTerms.def: An event that violates or imminently threatens security policy, requiring a coordinated response.
The phase of building the plan, team, tools, communications and training before an incident occurs.
The phase in which monitoring, alerts or reports first indicate a possible incident.
Confirming an incident is real and determining its scope, entry point, severity and required notifications.
Limiting the spread and impact of an incident, such as by isolating hosts and disabling accounts, while preserving evidence.
Removing the root cause, malware, persistence mechanisms and compromised credentials from the environment.
Restoring systems and data to normal operation from known-good sources and monitoring for recurrence.
The post-incident review that documents what happened and produces improvements fed back into preparation.
A communication channel separate from potentially compromised systems, such as a phone bridge or personal devices, used during response.

examTips: Know the seven phases in order: preparation, detection, analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned.
Isolating a host or disabling an account is containment; removing malware and patching is eradication; restoring from backup is recovery.
Anything done before an incident, such as training, playbooks and backups, belongs to preparation.
The post-incident meeting and report is lessons learned, and its output improves the next cycle.
videos.realWorld: During a ransomware attack on a mid-sized Nigerian bank, the SOC isolated 60 branch machines through EDR within twenty minutes of the first alert, which kept the core banking cluster clean. Analysis traced the entry to a vendor account on the VPN without MFA. Eradication removed a web shell on a reporting server the attacker had planted three weeks earlier, and recovery restored branch file shares from immutable backups. GRC filed the CBN incident report and the NDPC notification, and the lessons-learned actions included mandatory MFA for all third-party access and a monthly restore test.

quiz.q: An EDR alert shows a workstation encrypting files and attempting to spread to other systems. The analyst immediately isolates the host from the network and disables the user's account. Which incident response phase do these actions belong to?
quiz.explain: Isolating hosts and disabling accounts limit the spread of the incident, which is containment. Detection is the initial alert, eradication removes the cause, and recovery restores normal operation.

quiz.q: After a breach, the team removes a web shell, patches the exploited vulnerability and resets all service account credentials. Which phase is being performed?
quiz.explain: Removing the attacker's tools and persistence, closing the vulnerability and invalidating compromised credentials are eradication activities.

quiz.q: Two weeks after recovering from an incident, the security team meets to review the timeline, identify what slowed the response and assign improvement actions. Which phase is this and what does it feed into?
quiz.explain: The post-incident review is the lessons learned phase, and its output improves plans, tooling and training in the preparation phase, which is why incident response is drawn as a cycle.

videos.title: Incident Planning
videos.summary: Messer covers how to prepare the response capability: exercises such as tabletop sessions and simulations, root cause analysis, threat hunting, and the training that keeps the team ready.
videos.deepDive:
An incident response plan that has never been exercised is a document, not a capability. This video is about the activities that make the plan real: training people, testing the plan under realistic conditions, digging to the true root cause afterwards, and proactively hunting for intrusions rather than waiting for alerts.

Training. Everyone in the response chain needs role-specific training. Analysts practise triage, evidence handling and the specific tools. Incident managers practise coordination and decision-making under pressure. Executives, legal, communications and HR learn what decisions they will be asked to make (pay the ransom or not, when to notify customers) and what the regulators expect. Front-line staff learn how to recognise and report incidents and, importantly, what not to do, such as powering off a suspected machine before the SOC can capture memory, or discussing the incident on WhatsApp.

Testing: tabletop exercises. A tabletop is a discussion-based walkthrough. A facilitator presents a scenario in stages, for example: it is 09:00 Monday, the payment switch is unresponsive and a ransom note appears on the operations screens; twenty minutes later a journalist calls; an hour later the attacker emails a sample of customer data. At each stage the participants say what they would do, who they would call, and what authority they need. Tabletops are cheap, take a few hours, and are extremely effective at exposing gaps: nobody knows who can authorise disconnecting from the interbank network, the PR contact list is out of date, the backup administrator is on leave with no deputy. CBN expects banks to run these at least annually and to involve senior management.

Testing: simulations. A simulation exercises the technical response for real. This ranges from a controlled phishing campaign that measures click rates and reporting, to a red team or purple team engagement in which attackers emulate a real adversary while the SOC responds, to a full failover of the data centre to the disaster recovery site. Simulations validate that detections fire, that isolation actually works, that backups actually restore, and that people can execute the playbooks with the real tools. They are more expensive and must be scoped carefully so they do not become the incident, but they are the only way to know the plan works technically.

Root cause analysis (RCA). After an incident, the natural stopping point is the proximate cause: a user clicked a link. RCA keeps asking why until it reaches something the organisation can fix. Why did the click lead to compromise? Because macros were enabled. Why? Because the baseline GPO did not block them. Why? Because no one owned the Office hardening standard. Techniques include the five whys, fishbone diagrams and timeline reconstruction. The output is a small number of systemic fixes rather than blaming one person. RCA is what distinguishes an organisation that keeps having the same incident from one that stops having it.

Threat hunting. Detection waits for a rule to fire. Hunting assumes the attacker is already inside and goes looking. A hunt starts with a hypothesis drawn from threat intelligence or MITRE ATT&CK: if an attacker had compromised a service account, they would create scheduled tasks on domain controllers, so query every scheduled task created in the last 30 days and review the unusual ones. Hunters use EDR telemetry, SIEM data and network logs, and every hunt ends either with an incident or with a new detection rule so the SIEM catches it next time. Hunting is how organisations find intrusions that have been dwelling for months, and it is a core function of mature bank SOCs.

On the job. GRC analysts often own the exercise calendar, write the tabletop scenarios and track the corrective actions from RCAs. SOC analysts participate in simulations, run hunts between shifts, and convert hunt findings into detection content.

keyTerms.def: A discussion-based walkthrough of a scenario in which participants describe how they would respond, used to find gaps in plans and roles.
A hands-on exercise, such as a phishing test or red-team engagement, that tests the technical and procedural response for real.
A structured investigation that traces an incident past its immediate trigger to the underlying condition that allowed it.
An RCA technique that repeatedly asks why until a systemic, fixable cause is reached.
Proactively searching for signs of intrusion based on a hypothesis rather than waiting for alerts.
The specific attacker behaviour a hunt sets out to find, usually drawn from threat intelligence or MITRE ATT&CK.
A collaborative exercise in which attackers and defenders work together to test and improve detections.
The period between an attacker gaining access and being discovered, which hunting aims to shorten.

examTips: Tabletop is talk-through and low cost; simulation is hands-on and tests real tools. Pick tabletop when the question stresses decision-making or plan review, simulation when it stresses validating technical response.
Root cause analysis looks beyond the user who clicked to the control that was missing.
Threat hunting is proactive and hypothesis-driven; alert triage is reactive. If nothing has alerted but the team is searching anyway, it is hunting.
Training belongs to preparation; exercises validate preparation.
videos.realWorld: A Nigerian bank's GRC team runs a half-day tabletop with the executive committee: a simulated ransomware attack combined with a data extortion demand. The exercise reveals that no one could say who is authorised to engage the interbank switch to suspend outbound transfers, and that the incident communications template still names a former head of corporate affairs. Meanwhile the SOC's monthly hunt for unusual scheduled tasks on servers finds a persistence mechanism from a contractor's account that had been active for two months with no alert, which becomes both an incident and a new SIEM rule.

quiz.q: A bank wants senior management to walk through a ransomware scenario, discuss decision points such as regulatory notification and ransom payment, and identify gaps in the response plan, without affecting production systems. Which activity best fits?
quiz.explain: A tabletop is a discussion-based exercise ideal for testing decisions and plans with leadership at no technical risk. A simulation is hands-on, hunting looks for intrusions, and scanning finds vulnerabilities.

quiz.q: After a phishing incident, the initial report states the cause was an employee clicking a link. The security manager asks the team to determine why the click was able to lead to a compromise and what systemic change would prevent recurrence. Which activity is being requested?
quiz.explain: Going beyond the immediate trigger to the underlying control weakness is root cause analysis. Containment limits spread, hunting searches proactively for intrusions, and a simulation tests response.

quiz.q: No alerts have fired, but a SOC analyst reviews threat intelligence about a group targeting banks and begins searching EDR data for scheduled tasks and new services created on domain controllers during the past 60 days. Which activity is this?
quiz.explain: Proactively searching for attacker behaviour based on a hypothesis from intelligence, without any triggering alert, is threat hunting. Detection is alert-driven, and the other options are planning and review activities.

videos.title: Digital Forensics
videos.summary: Messer explains the forensic activities that support investigations and legal action: legal hold, chain of custody, acquisition, preservation, reporting and e-discovery.
videos.deepDive:
Digital forensics is the disciplined collection, preservation and analysis of digital evidence so that it can be trusted, in court, by a regulator or by the board. The difference between an investigation and a forensic investigation is that everything is done in a way that can be reproduced and defended later. Analysts will be asked to explain each step, so the process matters as much as the findings.

Legal hold. When litigation, a regulatory inquiry or a serious internal investigation is anticipated, legal counsel issues a legal hold: a formal instruction to preserve all potentially relevant data and to suspend normal deletion. That means mailbox retention policies are paused for named custodians, log rotation is stopped or logs are exported, backups scheduled for overwrite are kept, and departing employees' devices are not reimaged. Failing to preserve after a hold is issued can be treated as destruction of evidence, so the hold must be communicated in writing and its compliance tracked.

Chain of custody. Every piece of evidence needs a documented history from the moment it is collected. A chain of custody form typically records: a unique evidence identifier; a description (make, model, serial number, capacity of the drive, or the file name and hash for a logical export); date, time and location of collection; the name and signature of the person who collected it; the reason for collection; then a log of every transfer with date and time, released by, received by, and purpose (for example transported to forensic lab, imaged, returned to secure storage). Evidence is sealed in tamper-evident bags with the seal number recorded. If any link is missing, opposing counsel can argue the evidence was altered, and the whole case can fail on that point alone.

Acquisition. Collect evidence in order of volatility, most volatile first: CPU registers and cache, RAM, network connections and running processes, then disk, then removable media and backups, then paper. Memory capture before shutdown is essential because ransomware keys, injected code and attacker sessions live only in RAM. Disk acquisition uses a hardware write blocker so the source is never modified, and produces a bit-for-bit image (raw dd or E01 format). The examiner hashes the source and the image with SHA-256 and records both; matching hashes prove the copy is exact. For cloud services and mobile phones, acquisition often means API exports or vendor tools rather than physical imaging, and the same hashing and documentation applies. Everything is done on the image; the original is stored.

Preservation. Keep evidence intact and unaltered for as long as required: originals in locked, access-logged storage; working copies used for analysis; hashes re-verified periodically; and retention aligned with the legal hold and regulatory requirements. Preservation also covers ensuring timestamps are meaningful by recording the system clock offset from a reliable time source at collection.

Reporting. The forensic report describes what was collected, how, by whom, what tools and versions were used, what was found, and the analyst's conclusions, separating fact from interpretation. It must be understandable to a non-technical reader such as a judge or a bank's board, and reproducible by another examiner. Screenshots, hash lists and the chain of custody forms go in appendices.

E-discovery. Electronic discovery is the legal process of identifying, collecting, reviewing and producing electronically stored information for litigation or regulatory requests. It is broader than forensic imaging: it covers email, chat, documents and databases across many custodians, often using specialised platforms to search, deduplicate and tag for privilege before production. Forensics may feed e-discovery when authenticity of a specific item is disputed.

On the job. SOC analysts perform first-response acquisition (memory and triage images) under the guidance of a forensic lead and must fill in chain of custody forms correctly. GRC and legal teams issue legal holds, manage e-discovery for regulator or court requests, and retain forensic reports as part of incident records for CBN and NDPC.

keyTerms.def: A formal directive to preserve all potentially relevant data and suspend routine deletion when litigation or investigation is anticipated.
The documented record of who collected, handled, transferred and stored evidence, and when, proving it was not altered.
Collecting the most short-lived evidence first, such as memory and network state, before disk and backups.
A hardware or software device that allows reading a storage device while preventing any modification to it.
A bit-for-bit copy of a storage device, verified by hash, on which all analysis is performed instead of the original.
Computing a cryptographic hash of evidence at collection and later to prove it has not changed.
The legal process of identifying, collecting, reviewing and producing electronically stored information for litigation or regulators.
A reproducible, non-technical-readable document of evidence handling, methods, findings and conclusions.

examTips: Order of volatility: memory and network state before disk; if a question asks what to collect first from a running system, it is RAM.
Any question about proving evidence was not tampered with is answered by chain of custody plus hashing.
Legal hold is issued by legal counsel before or at the start of an investigation to stop deletion; it is not the same as a backup.
Always analyse a hashed image, never the original device, and use a write blocker for acquisition.
videos.realWorld: When a bank suspects an insider of exporting customer data, legal issues a hold covering the employee's mailbox, laptop and file-share activity. A SOC analyst captures the laptop's memory while it is still logged in, then images the drive through a write blocker, records SHA-256 hashes, seals the drive in an evidence bag and signs the chain of custody form before handing it to the forensic lead. Weeks later the report, with its hash verification and custody log, supports both the disciplinary process and a referral to law enforcement, and GRC produces the relevant emails through an e-discovery platform when the regulator asks.

quiz.q: A forensic analyst arrives at a running server suspected of compromise. Which evidence should be collected first?
options: A bit-for-bit image of the hard disk
The contents of system memory and active network connections
Backup tapes from the previous night
quiz.explain: The order of volatility requires capturing the most transient data first; RAM and network state are lost on shutdown, whereas disk, backups and paper persist.

quiz.q: During a court case, the defence argues that a hard drive presented as evidence may have been altered after seizure. Which documentation would best counter this argument?
options: The chain of custody form with hash values recorded at acquisition
quiz.explain: Chain of custody records every handler and transfer, and hashes taken at acquisition and re-verified later prove the evidence is unchanged. The other documents do not establish evidence integrity.

quiz.q: A company is notified that a customer intends to sue over a data breach. Which action should legal counsel take first to ensure relevant emails and logs are not deleted by routine retention policies?
options: Issue a legal hold to the relevant custodians and IT
Create a forensic image of every server
quiz.explain: A legal hold suspends normal deletion and preserves potentially relevant data as soon as litigation is anticipated. E-discovery comes later, imaging every server is impractical and unnecessary, and a lessons-learned report is unrelated to preservation.

objectives.title: Given a scenario, use data sources to support an investigation

videos.title: Log Data
videos.summary: Messer surveys the log types an investigator relies on: firewall, application, endpoint, OS-specific security, IPS/IDS and network infrastructure logs, plus the metadata hidden in files and emails. This note also covers the other investigation data sources in objective 4.9: vulnerability scans, automated reports, dashboards and packet captures.
videos.deepDive:
Every investigation is a reconstruction of what happened from records that systems left behind. Knowing which log holds which fact, and how to read it, is the everyday skill of a SOC analyst. The exam gives a scenario and asks which data source answers the question, so learn what each log contains.

Firewall logs. Each entry records time, source and destination IP, ports, protocol, the rule that matched and the action (allow or deny). Next-generation firewalls add application name, user, URL category and bytes transferred. Use them to answer: did the compromised host talk to the attacker's server, when did the first outbound connection occur, and what else in the network reached the same destination? A burst of denied outbound connections on unusual ports from one host is a strong beaconing indicator.

Application logs. Written by the application itself: web server access logs (client IP, request, status code, user agent), database audit logs (who ran which query), and core banking transaction logs. On Windows they appear in Event Viewer under Application; on Linux under /var/log, for example /var/log/apache2/access.log. A web access log showing hundreds of requests with SQL syntax in the query string and 500 errors is an injection attempt; a 200 after many 500s may be success.

Endpoint logs. Logon and logoff, process creation, service installation, USB insertion and software changes on the workstation or server, usually collected by the EDR agent or forwarded from the OS. These tell you what ran, under which account, and what it spawned.

OS-specific security logs. The Windows Security log is the richest single source. A failed logon looks like this: Event ID 4625, An account failed to log on. Account Name: jdoe, Logon Type: 3, Failure Reason: Unknown user name or bad password, Status: 0xC000006D, Sub Status: 0xC000006A, Workstation Name: WS-FIN-07, Source Network Address: 10.20.3.55. Read it as: a network logon (type 3, typically SMB or RPC; type 10 is Remote Desktop, type 2 is interactive at the keyboard) for jdoe failed because of a bad password (sub status 6A; 6A4 would mean the username does not exist), from address 10.20.3.55. Thousands of 4625 events for many usernames from one source in a few minutes is password spraying; the same for one username is brute force; a 4625 storm followed by a 4624 (successful logon) is the moment to worry. Other IDs worth memorising: 4624 successful logon, 4672 special privileges assigned (an admin logon), 4720 user account created, 4728 and 4732 member added to a privileged group, 4688 process created, 1102 audit log cleared, and 7045 new service installed. On Linux, /var/log/auth.log or /var/log/secure hold sshd and sudo events, and auditd records syscalls and SELinux denials.

IPS/IDS logs. Each alert names the signature that fired, its severity, source and destination, and often a packet excerpt. They tell you what attack was attempted and whether it was blocked (IPS) or only observed (IDS). Correlate with firewall and endpoint logs to see whether the attempt succeeded.

Network logs. Switches, routers, wireless controllers and VPN concentrators log configuration changes, interface state, routing updates, authentication successes and failures, and DHCP leases. NetFlow or sFlow records summarise every conversation (who talked to whom, how much, when) without payloads, which makes them ideal for spotting large transfers to unusual destinations. The VPN log tells you which user connected from which public IP at what time, which is often the pivot that links an external attacker to an internal account.

Metadata. Data about data: email headers showing every server a message passed through and the Authentication-Results; document properties showing author, organisation and last-saved-by; image EXIF data with camera model, timestamp and GPS location; browser and file system timestamps. Metadata often proves who created a file or where a phishing email really originated.

On the job. Analysts pivot between these sources constantly: a 4625 storm leads to the VPN log for the source, to the firewall for other destinations from that source, to EDR for what ran after the 4624. GRC ensures each source is retained for the periods CBN and PCI DSS require, typically at least a year with three months immediately searchable.

Beyond logs: the other data sources

Raw logs are the foundation, but an investigation also draws on processed and higher-level sources: the output of vulnerability scanners, scheduled reports, live dashboards and full packet captures. Each answers a different kind of question, and each has limits an analyst must understand. This video also explains why centralising all of it in a SIEM changes what is possible.

Vulnerability scans. A scanner such as Nessus, Qualys or OpenVAS produces a report per host listing detected vulnerabilities with CVE identifiers, CVSS scores, the evidence that triggered the finding, and remediation advice, along with configuration weaknesses such as missing patches, default credentials, unsupported operating systems, disabled host firewalls and out-of-date antivirus. During an investigation the scan history answers: was the exploited vulnerability known before the breach, when was it first reported, and was it marked as remediated? If the scan from three months earlier flagged the exact CVE the attacker used, the lessons-learned conversation is about patch management, not detection. Scans are also useful for scoping: every other host with the same vulnerability is a candidate for compromise and needs checking. Remember that a scan is a point-in-time picture and can produce false positives; confirm the finding on the host before drawing conclusions.

Automated reports. SIEMs, EDR platforms, identity systems and ticketing tools all generate scheduled reports: daily failed-logon summaries, weekly new privileged accounts, monthly firewall rule changes, top blocked domains, phishing simulation results. In an investigation they provide a baseline of what normal looked like. A report showing that the compromised account first appeared in the privileged-group-change list four weeks ago gives a timeline anchor that a live search may miss because the raw log has already rotated. For GRC, automated reports are audit evidence: proof that access reviews happened, that patch compliance was tracked, that the SOC monitored specific controls. The risk with reports is that nobody reads them; a report that shows the same warning every week for a year is a finding in itself.

Dashboards. A dashboard is a live, visual summary drawn from the SIEM or a monitoring tool: alerts by severity, top talkers, geographic map of logins, systems with failing backups, current open incidents. Analysts use dashboards for situational awareness at the start of a shift and during an incident to watch whether containment is working, for example a chart of outbound connections to the attacker's address dropping to zero after the firewall block. Dashboards are only as good as the queries behind them, so during a serious incident the team usually builds a dedicated incident dashboard tracking the specific indicators involved.

Packet captures. A packet capture (pcap) records every byte on a network segment, typically taken with tcpdump or Wireshark, from a SPAN port, a network tap, or a full-packet-capture appliance that keeps a rolling window. It is the ground truth: logs say a connection happened, the capture shows what was said. Analysts use it to extract a downloaded malware file, read an unencrypted credential, reconstruct the exact HTTP request that exploited a server, or confirm DNS tunnelling by seeing the encoded data in query names. Wireshark's follow-stream and protocol dissectors make this readable. The limits: encrypted traffic shows only metadata unless TLS inspection is in place, captures are enormous so they are usually kept only for hours or days, and capturing customer data raises NDPA obligations, so captures must be access-controlled and retained under policy.

Bringing it together. A SIEM ingests logs from every source over syslog, agents and APIs, normalises fields so that a source IP means the same thing whether it came from a firewall or a Linux server, correlates events across sources, alerts on rules, and keeps everything searchable. Time synchronisation via NTP across all sources is essential, because correlation across a firewall log, a Windows event and a pcap fails if clocks differ by minutes. Log retention must satisfy the longest applicable requirement; PCI DSS expects twelve months with three months readily available, and CBN examiners ask for evidence that logs are protected from tampering.

On the job. During a bank incident the analyst pulls the pcap for the initial exploitation, the scan history for the vulnerable server, and the dashboard to track containment, while GRC assembles the automated reports that show the control environment before the event for the regulator's incident file.
